label: The Circle and Its Fundamental Group
notes: This chapter delivers the first nontrivial fundamental group of the course. The angle on the circle is only a local coordinate, so we unwrap it with the exponential covering map and convert loop homotopy into ordinary endpoint arithmetic on the real line, producing the isomorphism with the integers.

label: The Exponential Covering Map
notes: The exponential map sends a real turn count to a point on the unit circle, and a unit shift in the source returns the same point. This periodicity is exactly why no continuous global angle exists, and it makes the real line an unwrapped model carrying infinitely many copies of every short arc.

label: Evenly Covered Arcs
notes: A short open arc pulls back to a disjoint union of intervals, and on each interval the exponential map restricts to a homeomorphism onto the arc. Inverting one such restriction gives a continuous local section, a single branch of angle valid on the arc but never on the whole circle at once.

label: Path Lifting
notes: Fix a real point above the starting circle point, and the path lifting property produces a unique continuous lift of the whole path. The lift is a running angle record measured in turns. Because the exponential map cannot see integer shifts, the lift remembers accumulated rotation that the circle itself discards.

label: Unique Lifting and Connectedness
notes: Two lifts of one map that agree at a single point must agree everywhere on a connected domain. The agreement set is open because nearby points share a sheet, and closed because disagreement also persists locally. Connectedness forces an all-or-nothing verdict, which is the engine behind every uniqueness claim in the chapter.

label: Homotopy Lifting
notes: Homotopies lift too, because the compact time interval is covered by finitely many evenly covered arcs that we lift strip by strip and glue using uniqueness. Endpoints held fixed downstairs stay fixed upstairs, so the lifted endpoint difference is a genuine invariant of the path homotopy class, not of one drawing.

label: Winding Number
notes: For a loop both lift endpoints lie in one fiber, so their difference is an integer called the winding number. Choosing a different lift only shifts both endpoints by a constant, leaving the difference unchanged, and homotopy lifting shows the integer is stable across the entire path homotopy class of the loop.

label: The Isomorphism with the Integers
notes: The standard once-around loop has lift the identity, so its winding number is one, and the n-fold loop lifts to n times the parameter. Concatenation adds endpoint differences, so winding number is a homomorphism that pairs with raising the generator to powers, giving the isomorphism between the fundamental group and the integers.

label: Degree of Circle Maps
notes: Every self-map of the circle carries one integer, the winding number of its composite with the standard loop, called its degree. Power maps have degree equal to their exponent, conjugation has degree minus one, rotations have degree one, and degree multiplies under composition while staying invariant under homotopy of the map.

label: No Retraction and Brouwer
notes: If the disk retracted onto its boundary circle, the boundary inclusion would induce an injection on fundamental groups, sending the integers into the trivial group, which is impossible. This no-retraction theorem immediately yields the two-dimensional Brouwer fixed point theorem by the standard ray-construction contradiction argument.

label: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
notes: A complex polynomial of positive degree restricted to a large circle winds around the origin as many times as its degree, while on a tiny circle it winds like its constant term. If the polynomial never vanished, the winding number would be homotopy invariant and constant, contradicting these two counts and forcing a root.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: The circle teaches the covering-space method and a single integer invariant that resurfaces everywhere. Evenly covered arcs supply lifts, connectedness supplies uniqueness, compactness supplies homotopy lifting, and the winding number supplies the isomorphism. The same integer becomes degree, drives fixed-point theorems, and previews higher-dimensional topology to come.
